Based on my analysis of the project files, I can now explain what $Chemistry is and its revolutionary approach to React development:
What is $Chemistry?
$Chemistry is a next-generation React framework that transforms React from a functional programming paradigm into a true object-oriented system. It's a complete abstraction layer that makes React components behave like classical OOP objects with real inheritance, polymorphism, and automatic state management.
The key innovation is the "children-as-constructor-arguments" pattern. When you write JSX like:
jsx
<Book>
    <Chapter title="Introduction" />
    <Chapter title="Main Content" />
</Book>
Chemistry transforms this into constructor calls where the Book receives actual Chapter instances, not just React elements. This creates a real object graph with bidirectional relationships.
Why $Chemistry Exists
The framework solves React's fundamental limitations:
No More Hook Complexity: No useState, useContext, useCallback, useEffect, or any hook rules. Just properties on classes that automatically trigger re-renders when changed.
True OOP in React: Classical inheritance works naturally. You can override methods like getCardStyle() or renderHeader() in subclasses, something impossible with React's functional components.
Automatic State Management: The $Reaction system tracks dependencies and updates automatically. No Redux, MobX, or Zustand needed - the object graph maintains itself.
Bidirectional Communication: Children know their parents and vice versa through the object graph. No prop drilling or context providers required.
Convention Over Configuration: The $ prefix elegantly distinguishes props from state. Methods become event handlers. Everything follows predictable patterns.
Where $Chemistry Lives (Architecture)
The framework consists of several key systems:
1. $Chemical Base Class
The foundation all components inherit from
Manages the component lifecycle and rendering
Provides the view() method (equivalent to React's render)
Handles parent-child relationships automatically
2. $Reaction System
Async state update orchestration with phases:
construction: Initial setup
formation: Building relationships
progress: Processing updates
process: Executing changes
destruction: Cleanup
Tracks which properties changed and updates only what's needed
Prevents unnecessary re-renders through intelligent dependency tracking
3. $Bond & $BondOrchestrator
Creates reactive bindings between properties and the DOM
Manages the "molecule" (context) system invisibly
Handles state propagation through the object graph
4. Component Generation
new $MyClass().Component creates a React component from your class
$use() provides instance binding for arrays and dynamic children
$bind() creates bound components with parent relationships
5. Type System
$Properties<T> and $$Properties<T> for type-safe props
$check() for runtime validation in constructors
Full TypeScript support with proper inference
Who $Chemistry is Written For
Primary Audience: Experienced React Developers
Developers who are frustrated with React's limitations and want:
Real OOP instead of functional programming gymnastics
Simpler state management without external libraries
Classical inheritance for UI component hierarchies
Freedom from hook rules and restrictions
Secondary Audience: Enterprise Teams
Teams building large-scale applications who need:
Predictable, maintainable code patterns
True modularity through inheritance
Reduced boilerplate and complexity
Better code reuse through polymorphism
Tertiary Audience: OOP Developers New to React
Developers coming from languages like Java, C#, or Python who find React's functional approach alien and want familiar OOP patterns.
The Revolutionary Insight
The core breakthrough is recognizing that React's JSX can be reinterpreted as constructor calls rather than just markup. This simple insight enables:
Polymorphic Components: A $Book can accept any $Chapter subclass
Dynamic Object Graphs: Components maintain real relationships
State as Properties: Just change this.count++ and it re-renders
Method Override Patterns: Subclasses can override rendering methods
Automatic Binding: No more this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this)
$Chemistry isn't just another state management library - it's a complete reimagining of how React applications should be built, bringing the power of classical OOP to the modern web while maintaining React's strengths in rendering and reconciliation.
The framework proves that the "binding problem" in UI development isn't about choosing between Angular's two-way binding or React's one-way flow - it's about having a proper object model where state naturally flows through real object relationships.

Key changes:
Lazy Loading: Used React.lazy() to dynamically import test components only when needed
No Default Selection: Changed useState('original') to useState<string | null>(null) so nothing loads initially
Welcome Screen: Added a welcome message when no test is selected (similar to the main page)
Suspense Boundary: Added loading state while a test component is being loaded
Uncommented All Tests: Since they won't run until selected, all tests can be available
Benefits:
Tests only execute when explicitly selected
Errors don't pile up from multiple tests
Better performance - only loads what's needed
Clear visual feedback during loading
Consistent UX with the main test runner
This pattern makes $Chemistry's test suite more accessible to all developers - from React veterans to complete beginners - by preventing confusing error cascades and providing a clean, guided experience!

Tests only load and execute when selected
No SSR issues with Chemistry's browser-dependent code
Automatic code splitting for better performance
Clean loading states without extra wrapper components

09:50 UTC, 26 October 2025
Looking at React's lifecycle phases and your Chemistry framework, here's how they map:
React's Actual Phases:
Render Phase - The component function executes, creating the virtual DOM
Commit Phase - React updates the actual DOM
Layout Phase - useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM updates
Paint - Browser paints to screen
Effect Phase - useEffect runs after paint
Mapping to Your $Chemistry Phases:
Looking at your phases in chemistry.ts:
typescript
type $Phase = 'construction' | 'formation' | 'progress' | 'process' | 'destruction';
Here's a suggested mapping:
␀0␀ → Component mount (useEffect with [] deps)
␀0␀ → Layout effects (useLayoutEffect) - forming DOM relationships
␀0␀ → The render function executing (creating VDOM)
␀0␀ → Effects after paint (useEffect) - processing side effects
␀0␀ → Component unmount (cleanup)
The Critical Question: What Phase is "Rendering"?
When the component function is running (your view() method), that's the Render Phase. This should probably map to your ␀1␀ phase since:
It's making progress toward the final UI
It shouldn't have side effects
It's where you're building the virtual DOM
Suggested Refactor:
Consider renaming for clarity:
typescript
type $Phase = 'mount' | 'layout' | 'render' | 'effect' | 'unmount';
Or keep your poetic names but be clear about the mapping:
typescript
class $Reaction {
    // During view() execution
    async progress() {  // This is "render" phase
        // Should NOT track or cause side effects
        // Just compute the view
    }
    
    // After DOM updates
    async formation() {  // This is "layout" phase
        // Can read DOM, make synchronous updates
    }
    
    // After paint
    async process() {  // This is "effect" phase  
        // Side effects, async operations
    }
}
The Infinite Loop Fix:
During the render phase (progress/when view() is running), you should:
NOT track property reads
NOT trigger updates
NOT modify state
This is likely your issue. Add a flag:
typescript
class $Reaction {
    private isRendering = false;
    
    async progress() {
        this.isRendering = true;
        try {
            const result = this.chemical.view();
            return result;
        } finally {
            this.isRendering = false;
        }
    }
    
    static track(chemical: $Chemical) {
        const reaction = chemical.__activeReaction;
        if (!reaction || reaction.isRendering) return; // NO tracking during render!
        // ...
    }
}
The key insight: During render phase, you're just computing what should appear, not causing effects!

Claude
09:52 UTC, 26 October 2025
You're absolutely right - "effect phase" is a weird React-ism that doesn't really make sense! Let's think about what's actually happening:
What React Really Does:
Render - Calculate what the UI should look like (pure computation)
Commit - Update the DOM to match
Browser Paint - Browser actually draws pixels
"Effects" - Really just "stuff that happens after painting"
The "effect phase" is a terrible name. It's really just "post-paint callbacks" - code that runs after the browser has painted, so it won't block the visual update.
For Your Chemistry Framework:
Your phases actually make MORE sense than React's:
typescript
type $Phase = 'construction' | 'formation' | 'progress' | 'process' | 'destruction';
␀0␀ - Building the chemical/component instance
␀0␀ - Forming bonds/relationships between chemicals
␀0␀ - Computing changes (like React's render)
␀0␀ - Processing reactions/updates
␀0␀ - Cleanup
The Real Question: When Should Things Run?
Instead of mapping to React's weird names, think about when you need things to happen:
typescript
class $Reaction {
    // BEFORE rendering - prep work
    async construction() {
        // Initialize, set up subscriptions
    }
    
    // DURING rendering - pure computation
    async progress() {
        // Compute view, but DON'T track or cause updates
        // This is where your infinite loop is happening!
    }
    
    // AFTER rendering - handle consequences  
    async process() {
        // Now you can track, update, cause reactions
    }
}
Your Infinite Loop Problem:
The issue isn't the phase names - it's that you're tracking during computation. You need:
typescript
class $Reaction {
    private computingView = false;
    
    async progress() {
        this.computingView = true;
        try {
            // While computing, DON'T track property access
            return await this.chemical.view();
        } finally {
            this.computingView = false;
        }
    }
    
    static track(chemical: $Chemical) {
        // Don't track while computing views!
        if (chemical.__activeReaction?.computingView) return;
        // ... rest of tracking
    }
}
Better Mental Model:
Think of it as:
Computation Phase (progress) - Figure out what to show, no side effects
Reaction Phase (process) - React to changes, cause updates
React's "effect" terminology is confusing because it makes you think about "side effects" when really it's just "deferred work". Your Chemistry framework can be clearer by focusing on what's actually happening: chemicals reacting to changes and forming bonds!

The Solution:
We need to decide what happens when someone misses their phase:
Option 1: Queue for Next Cycle
typescript
async layout() {
    if (this.phase === 'unmount') 
        return Promise.reject();
    
    // Already at or past layout phase
    if (this._phase === 'layout' || this._phase === 'effect') {
        // Either resolve immediately (already happened)
        // Or queue for NEXT render cycle
        console.warn('Layout called after layout phase - queueing for next render');
        return new Promise<void>(resolve => {
            this._render.push(() => {
                // Will run on next render, then proceed to layout
                this._layout.push(resolve);
            });
        });
    }
    
    return new Promise<void>(resolve => {
        this._layout.push(resolve);
    });
}
Option 2: Just Reject/Resolve Based on Timing
typescript
async layout() {
    if (this.phase === 'unmount') 
        return Promise.reject(new Error('Component unmounted'));
        
    // Too late - layout already happened
    if (this._phase === 'effect') 
        return Promise.reject(new Error('Layout phase already passed'));
        
    // Already in layout
    if (this._phase === 'layout') 
        return Promise.resolve();
    
    // Queue for when we reach layout
    return new Promise<void>(resolve => {
        this._layout.push(resolve);
    });
}
Option 3: Smart Phase Management (Recommended)
typescript
class $Reaction {
    private _phasePromises = new Map<$Phase, Promise<void>>();
    private _phaseResolvers = new Map<$Phase, (() => void)[]>();
    
    async waitForPhase(targetPhase: $Phase): Promise<void> {
        // Phase already passed in this cycle
        if (this.phaseOrder(targetPhase) < this.phaseOrder(this._phase)) {
            // Could either reject or queue for next cycle
            throw new Error(`Phase ${targetPhase} already passed (currently in ${this._phase})`);
        }
        
        // Currently in this phase
        if (this._phase === targetPhase) {
            return Promise.resolve();
        }
        
        // Queue for future phase
        if (!this._phasePromises.has(targetPhase)) {
            this._phasePromises.set(targetPhase, new Promise(resolve => {
                const resolvers = this._phaseResolvers.get(targetPhase) || [];
                resolvers.push(resolve);
                this._phaseResolvers.set(targetPhase, resolvers);
            }));
        }
        
        return this._phasePromises.get(targetPhase)!;
    }
    
    private phaseOrder(phase: $Phase): number {
        const order = { setup: 0, mount: 1, render: 2, layout: 3, effect: 4, unmount: 5 };
        return order[phase] || 0;
    }
    
    // Simplified phase methods
    async layout() {
        return this.waitForPhase('layout');
    }
    
    async effect() {
        return this.waitForPhase('effect');
    }
}

Get queued for the next render cycle explicitly

    if (workId && this._layoutWork.has(workId)) {
        return Promise.resolve();
    }
    
    // Do the work

        this._layout.push(() => {

            resolve();
        });

No, then() doesn't run synchronously! It's scheduled as a microtask. Here's the order:
javascript
console.log('1');

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log('3');  // Microtask
});

console.log('2');

// Output: 1, 2, 3
The then() callback is queued to the microtask queue and runs:
After all synchronous code completes
Before the next event loop iteration (before setTimeout, I/O, etc.)
So in your code:
typescript
if (this.phase === 'effect')
    this.effect().then(() => this.update());  // update() runs as a microtask
The this.update() won't run immediately - it waits for:
The current synchronous code to finish
Any other microtasks already in the queue
Then it runs (still in same event loop iteration)
This is actually good for your design! It means:
The update is deferred slightly (won't interrupt current execution)
But still happens "immediately" from the user's perspective (same event loop)
Multiple synchronous changes can batch before the update runs
If you needed truly synchronous execution, you'd have to use regular function calls, not promises. But the microtask timing is usually what you want for UI updates.

Looking at the validation test error and your $BondOrchestrator code, I can see the issue. The bound flag is likely causing problems when components are reused or when the bond process needs to run multiple times in the component tree.
The Problem:
In $BondOrchestrator:
typescript
bond(props: any, parentContext?: $BondOrchestrationContext): any {
    if (this.bound) return props;  // ← This exits early!
    // ... rest of bonding logic
    this.bound = true;  // ← Set after first run
}
Once bound is set to true, subsequent calls to bond() just return immediately without processing. But in a component tree, bond() might need to be called multiple times:
When the parent processes this component as a child
When the component itself renders
When props change
The Fix:
The bound flag should probably be scoped to a specific render cycle, not persistent across all calls. Try this:
typescript
class $BondOrchestrator<T extends $Chemical> {
    // Remove the persistent bound flag
    // bound = false;  ← DELETE THIS
    
    private _renderCycle = 0;
    private _lastBoundCycle = -1;
    
    render(props: any): ReactNode {
        this._renderCycle++;  // New render cycle
        
        const chemical = this._chemical;
        const reaction = chemical[$reaction];
        reaction.resolve('render');

        // Build the chemical
        this.bond(props);

        // Track the state of the reaction
        reaction.activate();
        const view = this.view();
        reaction.deactivate();
        reaction.updateIf();

        // Don't reset bound here
        return view;
    }

    bond(props: any, parentContext?: $BondOrchestrationContext): any {
        // Check if already bound in THIS render cycle
        if (this._lastBoundCycle === this._renderCycle) return props;
        this._lastBoundCycle = this._renderCycle;
        
        // ... rest of bonding logic stays the same
    }
}
Alternative: Remove the bound Optimization Entirely
If the above doesn't work, try removing the bound check completely:
typescript
bond(props: any, parentContext?: $BondOrchestrationContext): any {
    // if (this.bound) return props;  ← DELETE THIS LINE
    
    // ... rest of method
    
    // this.bound = true;  ← DELETE THIS LINE
    return props;
}
The optimization might be premature. React already handles avoiding unnecessary re-renders, and your _lastArguments check prevents re-running the constructor unnecessarily.

bond(props: any, parentContext?: $BondOrchestrationContext): any {
    const chemical = this._chemical;
    props = this.checkProps(props);
    let children: ReactNode = props.children;
    const context = new $BondOrchestrationContext(chemical, this._parameters);
    parentContext?.childContexts.push(context);

    this.process(children, context);

    if (!this.bound) {

        this.bindProps(chemical, props);

            children = context.build();
            props = { ...props, children: children || [] };

                $paramValidation.chemical = this._chemical;
                $paramValidation.paramCount = this._parameters.length;
                this._bondConstructor!.apply(this._chemical, context.arguments.values);
                this._lastAguments = context.arguments;
                $paramValidation.eval();
            }
        }
        
        this.bound = true;
    }
    
    return props;
}

Parent always collects child chemicals as constructor arguments

private processElement(element: React.ReactElement<any>, context: $BondOrchestrationContext) {

        // ... component creation code ...

        // Do this:
        if (context.parameter && context.parameterIndex >= 0 && context.parameterIndex < context.arguments.values.length) {

class $BondOrchestrationContext {

        this.args.push(value);
        
        // Also update the arguments object
        if (this.parameter && this.parameterIndex >= 0) {
            if (this.parameter.isSpread) {
                // For spread params, values go in the main array
                this.arguments.values.push(value);
            } else {
                // For regular params, set at the index
                this.arguments.values[this.parameterIndex] = value;
            }
        }
    }
}

14:31 UTC, 26 October 2025
You're touching on the core complexity here. Let me explain what's happening with tree rewriting in Chemistry:
How Tree Rewriting Works:
Parent processes children → Creates modified tree with bound Chemistry components
Parent's ␀0␀ renders → Returns React elements that might contain unbound components
␀0␀ replaces → Swaps unbound components with the pre-processed bound ones from step 1
The key is that when the parent rewrites its children, it creates a new tree where:
Chemistry components are replaced with bound versions (with correct keys/props)
<List> components are flattened into arrays
<Undefined> components are replaced with undefined
The Problem with Caching:

The Deep Problem of Tree Rewriting in Chemistry
React's rendering model assumes components are pure functions that transform props to elements. Each component is responsible for rendering its immediate children, creating a natural tree traversal where each node processes once. But Chemistry fundamentally breaks this model by introducing constructor arguments derived from children - a parent needs to inspect and transform its children before they render, collecting them as objects for its constructor while simultaneously preparing a modified tree for React to render.
The complexity emerges from React's reconciliation algorithm, which expects a stable tree structure where elements maintain referential identity across renders. When Chemistry rewrites the tree, it replaces React elements with new ones that have different keys, types, and props. This happens because Chemistry needs to transform <Chapter /> into a bound component with a chemical-based key like key="123" instead of whatever key (or lack thereof) the developer provided. React sees these as entirely different elements, triggering unmounts and remounts even when the logical component hasn't changed.
Your augmentView() method reveals the deeper issue: you're trying to intercept React's normal rendering flow. After the parent's view() method returns its React elements, you scan through them looking for Chemistry components that need replacement. This post-processing step is necessary because the view() method might create new component instances that weren't processed during the bonding phase. The parent might render <Chapter /> directly in its view, but that Chapter needs to be the bound version that was created during the bonding phase, not a fresh instance.
The N^2 problem you're avoiding with the bound flag is real and severe. Without it, every component in the tree would reprocess all its descendants on every render. A tree with depth D and branching factor B would process B^D nodes at the leaves, B^(D-1) at the next level up, and so on, leading to geometric growth in processing time. The bound flag acts as a circuit breaker, saying "I've already processed this subtree, don't do it again."
But here's where the fundamental tension arises: React's props flow is designed for immutability and referential transparency, while Chemistry's constructor pattern requires mutability and statefulness. When a parent's children change, React expects to just pass new props down. But Chemistry needs to re-collect those children as constructor arguments, potentially calling a different constructor signature. A component might have $Book(...chapters) as its constructor, and if the number of chapters changes, the entire constructor needs to be re-invoked with different arguments.
The validation tests expose this tension perfectly. The $ComplexValidator expects specific types in specific positions as constructor arguments. When you cache the tree withbound = true, you're also implicitly caching the constructor arguments. But if the parent passes different children - say, a $Book where a $Label was expected - the cached arguments don't match the current reality. The constructor still runs with the old arguments, leading to type mismatches.
React's Context API offers a hint at a solution pattern. Context separates data flow from component structure - providers and consumers can communicate without prop drilling. Similarly, Chemistry could separate argument collection from tree building. The bonding phase could be split into two passes: first, traverse the current children to collect constructor arguments, then separately decide whether to rebuild the tree structure. This would maintain the optimization while ensuring fresh data.
The challenge is that tree rebuilding and argument collection are currently intertwined in the process() method. When you encounter a <List> component, you both flatten it into an array (tree modification) and collect its children as arguments (data collection). When you see a Chemistry component, you both create a bound version with proper keys (tree modification) and push it to the context's arguments (data collection). Separating these concerns requires careful tracking of what needs to be done when.
Consider how React Fiber handles this problem. Fiber splits rendering into phases: the "render" phase walks the tree and builds a list of changes, while the "commit" phase applies those changes to the DOM. The render phase can be interrupted, resumed, or even thrown away, while the commit phase runs synchronously to completion. Chemistry could adopt a similar model: a "collection" phase that gathers arguments and a "construction" phase that builds the tree.
The _rendered map you maintain is trying to solve a related problem: ensuring that components created during bonding are reused in the augmented view. This map acts as a cache, but it's cleared on every fresh bond, meaning you lose the benefits of caching across renders. A more sophisticated approach might maintain a WeakMap keyed by the original React elements, allowing the cache to persist while still being garbage-collected when components unmount.
The deeper philosophical issue is that Chemistry is trying to make React's functional model behave like an object-oriented one. In OOP, parents know their children as objects with identity, state, and behavior. In React's functional model, children are just descriptions of what should be rendered. Chemistry bridges this gap by creating actual object instances (chemicals) that maintain identity across renders while still producing React's expected element descriptions.
Your current approach of checking if (this.bound) return props is too coarse-grained. It assumes that if the tree was built once, it never needs rebuilding. But children can change! A parent might render different children based on state, or children might be added/removed dynamically. One solution is to fingerprint the children. Create a hash or signature of the current children (their types, keys, and positions) and compare it to the last render. If the signature matches, you can safely reuse the cached tree. If it differs, you need to rebuild. This is similar to React's key prop - it helps identify when children have actually changed versus just re-rendered.
Another approach is to make argument collection lazy. Instead of collecting all arguments upfront, collect them on-demand when the constructor runs. This would require the constructor to pull arguments from the context rather than having them pushed as parameters. The trade-off is a less natural constructor signature, but it would eliminate the need to traverse children just for argument collection.
The ultimate solution might be to embrace React's model more fully. Instead of fighting React's rendering flow, work with it. Let each component be responsible for its own children, but provide a Chemistry-specific protocol for parent-child communication. This could be done through a Chemistry-aware context that manages the object graph independently of React's component tree. Parents and children would register with this context, establishing their relationships without requiring tree rewriting. What React Actually Does With Children
When a React component renders new children, React completely replaces the old children with the new ones. The parent's render function returns a new tree, and React's reconciliation algorithm compares this new tree with the previous tree to determine what changed. The old tree is effectively discarded - React doesn't "keep rendering" it. The new tree takes complete precedence.
This means when a parent component renders:
jsx
return <div>{condition ? <ChildA /> : <ChildB />}</div>
React will unmount ChildA and mount ChildB when the condition changes. The parent has total control over what renders.
Why You Added Tree Rewriting
Looking at your code, tree rewriting serves specific purposes:
Replacing unbound components with bound ones - When the parent's view() returns <Chapter />, that's just the unbound component. You need the bound version with the correct chemical instance and key.
Flattening ␀0␀ components - These are structural markers for your constructor arguments that shouldn't appear in the final React tree.
Processing ␀0␀ components - These pass undefined as constructor arguments but shouldn't render anything.
Assigning chemical-based keys - Each bound component needs key={chemicalId} for React's reconciliation.
What Happens Without Tree Rewriting
If you skip tree rewriting entirely and just collect constructor arguments, the parent's view() method would render unbound components. These would create new chemical instances on every render, breaking the object graph. Each <Chapter /> would be a fresh instance instead of the persistent chemical object that maintains state.
The Real Problem
You're trying to solve two problems at once:
Collecting chemicals as constructor arguments
Ensuring the rendered tree uses bound components
These are actually separate concerns. The constructor needs chemical objects, but the rendered tree needs bound React components that maintain chemical identity.
A Cleaner Solution
Instead of rewriting the tree during bonding, you could:

    bond(props: any, parentContext?: $BondOrchestrationContext): any {

    view(): ReactNode {

The Deeper Issue
Your current approach processes children during bonding to both collect arguments AND prepare the tree. But React will call render on those children anyway, making much of the tree preparation redundant. The children will render themselves - you don't need to pre-render them.
What you DO need is to ensure that when the parent's view() references a child component, it gets the bound version with the correct chemical instance. This is what augmentView() accomplishes by scanning the rendered tree and replacing components.
Why Caching Helps
Without the bound flag optimization, every component processes all its descendants. With caching, you skip reprocessing but need fresh arguments. The solution is to separate these:

Cache the augmentation map - Remember which components map to which chemicals
Reuse the map if children haven't changed - Skip reprocessing when possible

private $symbolize<T extends object>(target: T, visited = new Set()): T {

Unnecessary processing of immutable structures

For React elements, you need a stable identifier for state tracking. React elements don't have built-in IDs, but you can create a representation:
typescript
private $symbolize<T extends object>(target: T, visited = new Set()): T {
    if (!target || typeof target !== 'object') return target;
    if (visited.has(target)) return target;
    
    // Handle React elements - create a stable identifier
    if (React.isValidElement(target)) {
        const element = target as any;
        
        // Create a string representation
        const key = element.key || 'no-key';
        const type = typeof element.type === 'string' 
            ? element.type 
            : element.type?.name || 'Component';
        
        // Return a symbolized placeholder
        return {
            $$reactElement: true,
            $$key: key,
            $$type: type,
            $$id: `react-${type}-${key}`
        } as any;
    }
    
    visited.add(target);
    // ... rest of existing symbolize logic
}
Or use a WeakMap to cache React element IDs:
typescript
private reactElementIds = new WeakMap<React.ReactElement, number>();
private nextReactId = 0;

private $symbolize<T extends object>(target: T, visited = new Set()): T {
    if (React.isValidElement(target)) {
        let id = this.reactElementIds.get(target);
        if (!id) {
            id = this.nextReactId++;
            this.reactElementIds.set(target, id);
        }
        return { $$reactElementId: id } as any;
    }
    // ... rest of logic
}
This gives you a stable identifier without enumerating the React element's properties, avoiding the Next.js warnings while still allowing state tracking to work.

For a lightweight ID without enumerating properties, you can use the few properties React elements expose at the top level:
typescript
private $symbolize<T extends object>(target: T, visited = new Set()): T {
    if (React.isValidElement(target)) {
        const elem = target as any;
        
        // Use type and key to create identifier without deep enumeration
        const typeStr = typeof elem.type === 'string' 
            ? elem.type 
            : elem.type?.displayName || elem.type?.name || 'Unknown';
        
        const keyStr = elem.key !== null ? String(elem.key) : '';
        
        // Create a stable string without traversing props
        return `$$ReactElement:${typeStr}:${keyStr}` as any;
    }
    
    // ... rest of symbolize logic
}
This avoids:
Deep property enumeration (no Next.js warnings)
Accessing props object (which might contain params/searchParams)
Creating complex representations
You get a simple string like "␀0␀ReactElement:Book:item-1" that's sufficient for state tracking without triggering Next.js's overzealous warnings about parameter access.
The key insight: React elements are meant to be treated as opaque values. Just grab the minimal top-level info (type and key) without diving into props or children.

Component Identity in React: Persistence Across Renders, Unmounts, and Remounts
How React Tracks Component Identity
React's reconciliation algorithm determines component identity through a combination of element type and position in the tree. When React compares two element trees, it uses several rules:
Same Type, Same Position: If an element has the same type (e.g., div or MyComponent) in the same position, React considers it the same component instance and updates its props.
Different Type: If the type changes, React destroys the entire subtree and creates new component instances.
Different Position: Without keys, React matches elements by index. The first child in the old tree corresponds to the first child in the new tree.
This positional matching is why adding an item to the beginning of a list without keys causes all components to re-render with different props - React thinks each component has changed identity.
The Key Prop: React's Identity System
Keys are React's explicit identity system. When you provide a key prop, React uses it instead of position to match components across renders:
jsx
// Without keys - position-based matching
[<Item />, <Item />, <Item />]  // Components at indices 0, 1, 2

// With keys - identity-based matching  
[<Item key="a" />, <Item key="b" />, <Item key="c" />]
Keys must be:
Stable: The same component should have the same key across renders
Unique: Within a list, each key must be unique
Predictable: Not random (like Math.random()) which would cause remounting every render
When a key changes, React intentionally destroys the old component and creates a new one. This is used to force remounting:
jsx
<MyComponent key={resetCounter} />  // Changing resetCounter forces a new instance
Component Lifecycle and Identity Loss
Components lose identity in several scenarios:
Conditional Rendering: When a component is conditionally rendered, it's destroyed when hidden:
jsx
{show && <Component />}  // Component unmounts when show becomes false
Parent Remounting: When a parent unmounts, all children are destroyed:
jsx
{mode === 'a' ? <ParentA><Child /></ParentA> : <ParentB><Child /></ParentB>}
// Child is destroyed and recreated when mode changes
Type Changes: Even subtle type differences cause remounting:
jsx
const Comp1 = () => <div />;
const Comp2 = () => <div />;
{condition ? <Comp1 /> : <Comp2 />}  // Different types, different instances
Anonymous Functions: Creating components inside render causes new types each time:
jsx
function Parent() {
  const Child = () => <div />;  // New type every render!
  return <Child />;
}
State Persistence Strategies
1. Lift State Up
Move state to a parent that persists across the child's lifecycle:
jsx
function Parent() {
  const [childState, setChildState] = useState();
  return show ? <Child state={childState} setState={setChildState} /> : null;
}
2. Context for Cross-Tree Persistence
Context can maintain state even when components remount:
jsx
const StateContext = createContext();

function StateProvider({ children }) {
  const [persistentState, setPersistentState] = useState({});
  return (
    <StateContext.Provider value={{ persistentState, setPersistentState }}>
      {children}
    </StateContext.Provider>
  );
}
3. External State Management
Libraries like Redux, MobX, or Zustand store state outside React's component tree. Components can remount but reconnect to the same state.
4. DOM State Preservation
React 18's startTransition and Suspense can preserve DOM state during transitions, but this doesn't preserve component instances - just the DOM nodes.
5. Portal Tricks
Portals can move components in the DOM without unmounting:
jsx
const cache = useRef({});
function PersistentComponent({ id, children }) {
  if (!cache.current[id]) {
    cache.current[id] = createPortal(children, document.body);
  }
  return cache.current[id];
}
React's Fiber Architecture and Identity
React Fiber maintains a work-in-progress tree and a current tree. Each fiber node has:
type: The component type
key: The key prop
stateNode: The component instance (for class components) or DOM node
memoizedState: Hook state for function components
When reconciling, React tries to reuse fibers by matching type and key. If matched, it preserves memoizedState, maintaining hook state across renders.
Community Solutions
React Query / SWR
These libraries cache async state outside components, allowing data to persist across unmounts:
jsx
const { data } = useQuery(['todos'], fetchTodos);
// Data persists in cache even if component unmounts
React-Keep-Alive
Community packages attempt to preserve component instances similar to Vue's keep-alive:
jsx
<KeepAlive name="my-component">
  <ExpensiveComponent />
</KeepAlive>
These work by hiding components instead of unmounting them, but this can cause memory leaks and doesn't work with React's Suspense boundaries.
Application to Chemistry Framework
For your Chemistry framework, the async bond problem occurs because:
Async operations in the bond constructor might complete after the component unmounts
The component might remount with a fresh instance before async work completes
The bond established asynchronously points to a destroyed chemical
Potential solutions:
Chemical Instance Registry
Maintain a global registry mapping stable IDs to chemical instances:
typescript
class ChemicalRegistry {
  private chemicals = new Map<string, $Chemical>();
  
  getOrCreate(type: typeof $Chemical, key: string, parent?: $Chemical): $Chemical {
    const id = `${type.name}-${key}-${parent?.$cid || 'root'}`;
    if (!this.chemicals.has(id)) {
      this.chemicals.set(id, new type());
    }
    return this.chemicals.get(id)!;
  }
}
Stable Keys from Props
Generate stable keys from props to identify "same" components:
typescript
function getChemicalKey(type: typeof $Chemical, props: any): string {
  // Use props that identify this instance
  return `${type.name}-${props.id || props.key || JSON.stringify(props)}`;
}
Parent-Child Relationship Tracking
Since chemicals know their parents, you can use the parent chain as identity:
typescript
class $Chemical {
  getIdentityPath(): string {
    if (!this.parent) return `root-${this[$type].name}`;
    return `${this.parent.getIdentityPath()}-${this[$type].name}-${this.indexInParent}`;
  }
}
Deferred Bonding
Instead of async bonding during construction, defer until after mount:
typescript
class $BondOrchestrator {
  async bond(props: any) {
    if (this.phase !== 'mounted') {
      this.deferredBonds.push(() => this.bond(props));
      return;
    }
    // Perform actual bonding
  }
}
The fundamental challenge is that React's identity system (keys and types) operates at the element level, while Chemistry needs identity at the object level. Bridging this gap requires maintaining your own identity system that survives React's reconciliation while respecting React's rules about when components should genuinely be new instances.

Here's the rewritten augmentView and augmentNode methods that traverse the tree and fix chemical component keys:
typescript
private augmentView(view: ReactNode): ReactNode {
    const augmented = this.augmentNode(view);
    return React.createElement(
        React.Fragment,
        { key: `chem-${this._chemical[$cid]}` },
        augmented,
    );
}

private augmentNode(node: ReactNode): ReactNode {
    if (!node) return node;
    
    if (React.isValidElement(node)) {
        const element = node as React.ReactElement;
        const type = element.type as any;
        
        // Check if this is a Chemistry component with a chemical
        if (typeof type === 'function' && type.$chemical) {
            const chemical = type.$chemical;
            const correctKey = `${chemical[$cid]}`;
            
            // Check if key needs updating
            if (element.key !== correctKey) {
                // Clone with correct key and recursively process children
                const children = (element.props as any)?.children;
                const augmentedChildren = children ? 
                    React.Children.map(children, child => this.augmentNode(child)) : 
                    undefined;
                
                return React.cloneElement(
                    element, 
                    { ...element.props, key: correctKey },
                    augmentedChildren
                );
            }
        }
        
        // For non-Chemical elements or correctly keyed chemicals, just recurse on children
        const children = (element.props as any)?.children;
        if (children) {
            const augmentedChildren = React.Children.map(children, child => this.augmentNode(child));
            if (augmentedChildren !== children) {
                return React.cloneElement(element, element.props, augmentedChildren);
            }
        }
        
        return node;
    }
    
    if (Array.isArray(node)) {
        let changed = false;
        const augmented = node.map(child => {
            const aug = this.augmentNode(child);
            changed = changed || (aug !== child);
            return aug;
        });
        return changed ? augmented : node;
    }
    
    return node;
}
Key changes:
Checks if type.$chemical exists to identify Chemistry components
Gets the correct key from chemical[$cid]
Compares current key with correct key
If different, clones the element with the correct key
Always recursively processes children to catch nested chemicals
Removed the _rendered map check since we're now focusing on key correction
This ensures all Chemistry components in the rendered tree have stable keys based on their chemical ID, which should help maintain identity across renders and prevent unwanted remounting.

typescript
private augmentView(view: ReactNode): ReactNode {
    const augmented = this.augmentNode(view);
    return React.createElement(
        React.Fragment,
        { key: this._chemical[$symbol] },

    );

private augmentNode(node: ReactNode): ReactNode {
    if (!node) return node;
    
    if (React.isValidElement(node)) {
        const element = node as React.ReactElement;
        const type = element.type as any;
        
        // Check if this is a Chemistry component that needs key correction
        if (typeof type === 'function' && type.$chemical) {
            const chemical = type.$chemical;
            const correctKey = chemical[$symbol];
            
            if (element.key === correctKey) {
                // Key is already correct, just recurse on children
                const children = (element.props as any)?.children;
                if (!children) return node;
                
                const augmentedChildren = React.Children.map(children, child => this.augmentNode(child));
                if (augmentedChildren === children) return node;
                
                return React.cloneElement(element, element.props, augmentedChildren);
            }
            
            // Key needs updating
            const children = (element.props as any)?.children;
            const augmentedChildren = children ? 
                React.Children.map(children, child => this.augmentNode(child)) : 
                undefined;
            
            // Key is the second argument, not in props!
            return React.cloneElement(element, { key: correctKey }, augmentedChildren);
        }
        
        // Non-Chemical element - just process children
        const children = (element.props as any)?.children;
        if (!children) return node;
        
        const augmentedChildren = React.Children.map(children, child => this.augmentNode(child));
        if (augmentedChildren === children) return node;
        
        return React.cloneElement(element, element.props, augmentedChildren);
    }
    
    if (Array.isArray(node)) {
        let changed = false;
        const augmented = node.map(child => {
            const aug = this.augmentNode(child);
            changed ||= (aug !== child);
            return aug;
        });
        return changed ? augmented : node;
    }
    
    return node;
}

    private _active?: Promise<any>;

        this._isProp = false;
        this._isMethod = true;
        this._isPure = $Bond.isSpecial(method);

        if (this.initialized) return;
        this._initialized = true;
        if (this.skip()) return;
        
        const property = this._property;
        const descriptor = this._descriptor;
        const chemical = this._chemical;

        this._action = descriptor.value.bind(chemical);
        this._bondDescriptor = {
            value: (...args: any[]) => {
                return this.bondForm(...args);
            },
            writable: true,
            enumerable: true,
            configurable: true,

                return this.lastSeenValue;
            this._lastSeenArgs = argSymbol;

            reaction.activate('existing');

            let result = this.action!(...args);
            if (!(result instanceof Promise)) {
                this.lastSeenValue = result;
                return result;
            }
            return this.handleAsync(result);
        } finally {
            if (updateRequired) {
                reaction!.deactivate();
                reaction!.updateIf();
            }
        }
    }

    protected handleAsync(action: Promise<any>): $Promise<any> {
        this._isAsync = true;
        this._lastSeenValue = undefined;

            if (this._active != action) return;
            this._active = undefined;
            this.lastSeenValue = result;
            this._lastSeenAction!.result = result;
        }) as $Promise<any>;
        this._active = action;
        this._lastSeenAction.result = this._lastSeenValue;
        return this._lastSeenAction;
    }
}

You're right that promises can't be truly cancelled in JavaScript - they'll complete regardless. For handling the "last call wins" semantics with non-pure async methods, you have a few conceptual approaches:
Generation/Version tracking: Each call gets an incrementing number. When the promise resolves, check if it's still the latest generation before applying side effects. Earlier calls that complete later see they're outdated and skip their side effects.
AbortController pattern: While you can't cancel arbitrary promises, you could have your async methods check an abort signal at key points. This requires cooperation from the async function itself though.
Acceptance: Just document that for non-pure async methods, the last-to-complete wins, not last-to-start. This is actually predictable behavior that developers can reason about.
Split the concerns: Separate the "trigger render" concern from the "update value" concern. Maybe all completed promises update a value map, but only the most recent triggers a render.
The core tension is that JavaScript promises represent "eventual values" not "cancellable operations". Once you've started an async operation (like a network request or timer), it's going to complete. The best you can do is decide whether to ignore its result when it arrives.
For your framework, generation tracking seems most aligned with your goals - you want predictable behavior where the most recent user action takes precedence, even if an earlier action completes later.

12:33 UTC, 27 October 2025
You're correct - you can't bracket an async method with synchronous context or prevent its side effects from occurring once it starts executing. This is a fundamental limitation of JavaScript's async execution model.
Once an async method starts running, its code will execute and any side effects (setting properties, calling other methods, manipulating DOM, etc.) will happen regardless. You have no synchronous wrapper around the async execution - each await point is a yield to the event loop where anything can happen.
Your options are fundamentally limited:
Serialization: Queue async method calls so only one runs at a time. This guarantees predictable ordering but sacrifices concurrency:
typescript
if (this._activeQueue) {
    return this._activeQueue = this._activeQueue.then(() => this.action(...args));
}
this._activeQueue = this.action(...args);
Accept the chaos: Document that concurrent non-pure async methods will have interleaved side effects. This is what most frameworks do - concurrent mutations lead to unpredictable state.
Cooperative cancellation: Require async methods to check a cancellation token at key points. But this only works if the method author cooperates:
typescript
async myMethod(token) {
    await step1();
    if (token.cancelled) return;
    await step2();
    if (token.cancelled) return;
    // etc
}
The fundamental issue is that Chemistry can't control what happens inside user-defined async methods. Onceawait yields control, the method will resume and continue executing its side effects. There's no way to "reach into" an executing async function and stop it.
This is why most reactive frameworks either serialize updates or accept that concurrent async operations lead to race conditions. You're hitting the boundary of what's possible in JavaScript's execution model.

You're onto something with the hook points. Since Chemistry controls what render() and effect() return, you could make them throw or never resolve for cancelled operations:
typescript
async render() {
    if (this.generation !== currentGeneration) {
        throw new CancellationError();  // Stop execution here
        // Or: return new Promise(() => {}); // Never resolve
    }
    // Normal render logic
}
This would halt the async method at that await point. Any code after await this.render() wouldn't execute for cancelled calls.
However, this approach has limitations:
Partial execution: Everything before the first await this.render() or await this.effect() still executes. Side effects in that portion can't be prevented.
Error handling: If the user wraps their awaits in try/catch, they'll catch your cancellation and might continue anyway.
Multiple paths: If the method has conditional logic that might skip your hook points, those paths execute fully:
typescript
async myMethod() {
    this.someProperty = 1;  // Always happens
    if (condition) {
        await this.render();  // Might not reach this
    }
    this.otherProperty = 2;  // Happens if condition is false
}
Unhandled rejections: Throwing from render() creates rejected promises that might trigger unhandled rejection warnings if the calling code doesn't handle them.
The most robust approach might be to return a special "cancelled" promise that looks successful but signals cancellation through a property or symbol, letting the rest of the method complete but marking its results as outdated. But this still doesn't prevent side effects, just helps track which results to ignore.

Promise cancellation in JavaScript is a pattern, not a built-in feature. Here's how it typically works:
AbortController Pattern:
typescript
protected handleAsync(action: Promise<any>): $Promise<any> {
    // Cancel previous if exists
    if (this._abortController) {
        this._abortController.abort();
    }
    
    this._abortController = new AbortController();
    const signal = this._abortController.signal;
    
    const $action = action.then(async result => {
        if (signal.aborted) return;  // Check at start
        
        // ... do work ...
        
        if (signal.aborted) return;  // Check before render
        await this.chemical.render();
        
        if (signal.aborted) return;  // Check after render
        this.lastSeenValue = result;
    });
}
But here's the problem: the original action promise (the user's async method) is already running. You're only wrapping its .then() handler. The user's method body executes regardless.
What you can actually control:
First call: Executes completely, you learn it's async
Second call: You can prevent YOUR handling (the render, the value update) but NOT the method itself
The method's side effects: Still happen no matter what
The "cancellable promise" libraries typically work by:
Throwing a special error that propagates through the chain
Checking a flag at various points
Never resolving (creating a memory leak)
But none of these stop an already-executing async function. If the user wrote:
typescript
async doThing() {
    this.x = 1;  // Happens
    await delay(100);  // Can't stop this
    this.y = 2;  // Will happen unless you intercept at delay
}
You can't prevent this.y = 2 from executing unless you control what delay returns. Since you control render() and effect(), you could make those throw or never resolve for cancelled operations, but any other await points are out of your control.
The harsh reality: true cancellation requires cooperation from the async function itself. Without that, you're just deciding whether to ignore the results, not preventing the execution.

The resolve/reject functions in a Promise constructor only control the promise's state, not the execution of code:
javascript
new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    console.log('1');
    reject(new Error('stop!'));
    console.log('2');  // This still runs!
});
More importantly, when you have an async function like:
javascript
async function userMethod() {
    this.x = 1;
    await someDelay();
    this.y = 2;  // This will run regardless
}
The promise returned by userMethod() is created by JavaScript's async/await machinery. You don't have access to its internal resolve/reject functions. You can't "reach in" and reject it from outside.
When you do userMethod().then(...), you're attaching handlers to an already-created promise. Rejecting in your .then() handler creates a NEW rejected promise in the chain, but doesn't stop the original async function:
javascript
const promise = userMethod();  // Already running
promise.then(result => {
    throw new Error('reject!');  // Only affects promises chained after this
});
// userMethod is still running, still setting this.y = 2
The async function continues executing until it hits a return, throw, or reaches the end. Nothing you do from outside can stop it mid-execution except:
Making one of its await points throw (which you can only do if you control what it's awaiting)
Having it check a cancellation flag that you set (requires cooperation)
This is why your idea about controlling render() and effect() is actually your best bet - you control those await points.

Yes, you can return a cancellable promise wrapper to prevent downstream effects! You control what the caller sees:
typescript
protected handleAsync(action: Promise<any>): $Promise<any> {
    this._isAsync = true;
    
    // Create a cancellable wrapper
    let cancelled = false;
    const $action = Object.assign(
        action.then(async result => {
            if (cancelled) return;  // Don't process if cancelled
            
            // Your handling code
            await this.chemical.render();
            this.lastSeenValue = result;
            return result;
        }),
        { 
            cancel: () => { cancelled = true; }
        }
    ) as $Promise<any>;
    
    // Cancel previous if exists
    if (this._lastSeenActive?.cancel) {
        this._lastSeenActive.cancel();
    }
    
    this._lastSeenActive = $action;
    return $action;
}
Now when a new call comes in, you cancel the previous wrapper. The original async method still runs to completion, but:
It won't update lastSeenValue
It won't trigger renders
Any code chained to the returned promise won't execute
The caller gets back what looks like a promise but has a cancel() method. If they chain more .then() calls, those won't run if cancelled.
This doesn't stop the user's method from running its side effects, but it stops YOUR framework from propagating those effects (renders, state updates, etc.). It's damage control - you can't prevent the wound but you can stop the bleeding.

You can create a cancellable promise by storing the reject function outside the promise constructor:
typescript
protected handleAsync(action: Promise<any>): $Promise<any> {
    this._isAsync = true;
    
    let rejectFn: ((reason?: any) => void) | undefined;
    
    // Create a race between the original action and a cancellation promise
    const cancellationPromise = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
        rejectFn = reject;
    });
    
    const $action = Object.assign(
        Promise.race([
            action.then(async result => {
                // Your handling code
                await this.chemical.render();
                this.lastSeenValue = result;
                return result;
            }),
            cancellationPromise
        ]),
        {
            cancel: () => rejectFn?.(new Error('Cancelled'))
        }
    ) as $Promise<any>;
    
    // Cancel previous if exists
    if (this._lastSeenActive?.cancel) {
        this._lastSeenActive.cancel();
    }
    
    this._lastSeenActive = $action;
    return $action;
}
Promise.race resolves/rejects with whichever promise settles first. When you call cancel(), it rejects the cancellation promise, which causes the race to reject immediately, even if the original action is still running.
The original async method still executes to completion, but anyone awaiting your returned promise will get a rejection when cancelled.

async unmount(cancel?: () => void) {
    if (this._phase === 'unmount') 
        return Promise.resolve();

But wait - that's modifying the passed-in cancel function, which is weird. Better approach:
typescript
async unmount(): Promise<void & { cancel?: () => void }> {
    if (this._phase === 'unmount') 
        return Promise.resolve();
    
    let rejectFn: ((reason?: any) => void) | undefined;
    
    const promise = new Promise<void>((resolve, reject) => {
        rejectFn = reject;
        this._unmount.push(resolve);
    });
    
    // Attach cancel method to the promise
    return Object.assign(promise, {
        cancel: () => rejectFn?.(new Error('Unmount cancelled'))
    });
}
Now callers can do:
typescript
const unmountPromise = await this.unmount();
// Later...
unmountPromise.cancel?.();
This creates a promise that can be cancelled by calling the cancel method attached to it. When cancelled, it rejects, preventing any code after the await from executing.

Here's a utility function to create cancellable promises with result tracking:
typescript
function $promise<T = any>(
    executor: (resolve: (value: T) => void, reject: (reason?: any) => void) => void
): $Promise<T> {
    let rejectFn: ((reason?: any) => void) | undefined;
    let result: T | undefined;
    
    const promise = new Promise<T>((resolve, reject) => {
        rejectFn = reject;
        
        // Wrap resolve to capture result
        const wrappedResolve = (value: T) => {
            result = value;
            resolve(value);
        };
        
        executor(wrappedResolve, reject);
    });
    
    return Object.assign(promise, {
        get result() { return result as T; },
        cancel: () => rejectFn?.(new Error('Cancelled'))
    }) as $Promise<T>;
}
Usage:
typescript
const myPromise = $promise<string>((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => resolve('done'), 1000);
});

// Later:
myPromise.cancel();  // Rejects the promise
// or
await myPromise;
console.log(myPromise.result);  // 'done'
This gives you promises that:
Track their result value when resolved
Can be cancelled from outside
Work with async/await normally
Type-safe with generics

export function $promise<T = any>(executor: (resolve: (value?: T) => void) => void): $Promise<T> {
    let cancel: ((reason?: any) => void) | undefined;
    const promise = new Promise<T>((resolve, reject) => {
        cancel = reject;
        executor(resolve as any);
    }) as $Promise<T>;
    
    promise.cancel = () => cancel?.();
    
    const originalThen = promise.then.bind(promise);
    promise.then = function<U>(onFulfilled?: (value: T) => U | PromiseLike<U>, onRejected?: any): $Promise<U> {
        const chained = $promise<U>(resolve => {
            originalThen(value => {
                promise.result = value;
                const result = onFulfilled?.(value) ?? value;
                if (result instanceof Promise) {
                    result.then(resolve);
                } else {
                    resolve(result as U);
                }
            }, onRejected);
        });
        
        const chainedCancel = chained.cancel;
        chained.cancel = () => {
            chainedCancel();
            promise.cancel();
        };
        
        return chained;
    };
    
    return promise;
}

Here's a more complete version that's still elegant:
typescript
export function $promise<T = any>(executor: (resolve: (value?: T) => void) => void): $Promise<T> {
    let reject: ((reason?: any) => void) | undefined;
    let promise = new Promise<T>((res, rej) => {
        reject = rej;
        executor(res as any);
    }) as $Promise<T>;
    
    promise = promise.then(value => { promise.result = value; return value; }) as $Promise<T>;
    const originalThen = promise.then.bind(promise);

    promise.cancel = () => reject?.();
    promise.then = function<U>(onFulfilled?: (value: T) => U, onRejected?: any): $Promise<U> {
        const next = $promise<U>(resolve => {
            originalThen(
                value => {
                    if (!onFulfilled) return resolve(value as any);
                    const result = onFulfilled(value);
                    Promise.resolve(result).then(resolve);
                },
                onRejected
            );
        });
        
        const nextCancel = next.cancel;
        next.cancel = () => {
            nextCancel();
            promise.cancel();
        };
        return next;
    } as any;
    return promise;
}
This adds the onRejected parameter so error chains work properly. The cancellation still cascades as intended.

export function $promise<T = any>(executor: (resolve: (value?: T) => void) => void): $Promise<T> {
    let reject: ((reason?: any) => void) | undefined;
    let promise = new Promise<T>((res, rej) => {
        reject = rej;
        executor(res as any);
    }) as $Promise<T>;
    
    promise = promise.then(value => { promise.result = value; return value; }) as $Promise<T>;
    const then = promise.then.bind(promise);

    promise.cancel = (action?: () => any) => { reject?.(); action?.(); }
    promise.then = function<U>(onFulfilled?: (value: T) => U, onRejected?: any): $Promise<U> {
        const next = $promise<U>(resolve => {
            then(
                value => {
                    if (!onFulfilled) return resolve(value as any);
                    const result = onFulfilled(value);
                    Promise.resolve(result).then(resolve);
                },
                onRejected
            );
        });
        
        const cancel = next.cancel;
        next.cancel = (action?: () => any) => {
            cancel(action);
            promise.cancel(action);
        };
        return next;
    } as any;
    return promise;
}

Only the most recent call gets to trigger render

For pure async methods: Yes, they bypass all this complexity. The early return in bondForm when args match means:
First call with args X starts the async operation
Subsequent calls with same args return the same promise (_lastSeenActive)
Once complete, subsequent calls return the cached value
No re-execution, no render cascades
The cancel action semantics are subtle - when you cancel a promise chain, the action gets called multiple times (once per level in the chain) because of how cancel cascades. This might cause unexpected side effects if the action isn't idempotent.
The approach handles the common case well: rapid calls to the same async method where you want only the latest to trigger UI updates but still want all results captured. But the value race condition for non-pure methods might surprise users - the displayed value might not match the last call made.

Here's the updated implementation with cancellation token support:
typescript
const $cancelled = Symbol('$promise.cancelled');

export function $promise<T = any>(executor: (resolve: (value?: T) => void) => void): $Promise<T> {
    let reject: ((reason?: any) => void) | undefined;
    let promise = new Promise<T>((res, rej) => {
        reject = rej;
        executor(res as any);
    }) as $Promise<T>;
    
    promise = promise.then(value => { promise.result = value; return value; })
        .catch(err => {
            if (err === $cancelled) return undefined as T;
            throw err;
        }) as $Promise<T>;
    
    const then = promise.then.bind(promise);

    promise.cancel = (action?: () => any) => { reject?.($cancelled); action?.(); }
    promise.then = function<U>(onFulfilled?: (value: T) => U, onRejected?: any): $Promise<U> {
        const next = $promise<U>(resolve => {
            then(
                value => {
                    if (!onFulfilled) return resolve(value as any);
                    const result = onFulfilled(value);
                    Promise.resolve(result).then(resolve);
                },
                err => {
                    if (err === $cancelled) return reject?.(err);
                    if (onRejected) return onRejected(err);
                    throw err;
                }
            );
        });
        
        const cancel = next.cancel;
        next.cancel = (action?: () => any) => {
            cancel(action);
            promise.cancel(action);
        };
        return next;
    } as any;
    return promise;
}
The key changes:
Cancel now rejects with $cancelled token
Added catch after the initial then to suppress cancellation from becoming an unhandled rejection
Modified the error handler in the overridden then to pass cancellation through the chain without treating it as an error
This way cancellation flows through the chain but doesn't trigger Next.js error reporting.

The framework semantics are:
$ methods are pure - same args should return cached results
Constructors can call $ methods freely since they're cached
This enables declarative code that "looks" like it runs every time but actually caches

The Next.js warnings are happening because your $symbolize function (in $Represent.safe) is enumerating object properties, and Next.js 15 is mistakenly thinking you're accessing routeparams or searchParams without proper async handling.
Looking at the stack trace, the issue is at line 1906 in chemistry.ts:
typescript
for (const k in val) {
When $lookup is called in your loading tests, it likely uses $symbolize internally. If any object being symbolized has properties named "params" or "searchParams" (or Next.js detects patterns it thinks are route parameters), it triggers these warnings.
The issue is that Next.js 15 added aggressive detection for synchronous parameter access, and it's getting false positives from your serialization code. Your code isn't actually accessing route parameters - it's just iterating over object properties for serialization.
Some potential solutions:
Suppress the warnings for $symbolize: Add a check to skip certain property names:
typescript
for (const k in val) {
    if (k === 'params' || k === 'searchParams') continue;
    // ... rest of processing
}
Use Object.keys() instead of for...in: Sometimes this avoids triggering Next.js's detection:
typescript
Object.keys(val).forEach(k => {
    const processed = process(val[k], replacer);
    // ...
});
Check what objects are being symbolized: Add logging to see what's being passed to $symbolize that might contain params/searchParams properties.
The warnings themselves aren't breaking anything - they're false positives from Next.js's overly aggressive detection. But they're annoying and cluttering your console.

What are the view directives? Why do people like them?
Claude
15:46 UTC, 27 October 2025
Vue and Angular directives are template-level instructions that modify DOM elements declaratively. They're popular because they let developers express common patterns concisely in templates rather than in component logic.
Common directives include:
Conditional rendering: Vue's v-if / Angular's *ngIf - show/hide elements based on conditions List rendering: Vue's v-for / Angular's *ngFor - repeat elements for arrays Two-way binding: Vue's v-model / Angular's [(ngModel)] - sync form inputs with data Event handling: Vue's v-on / Angular's (click) - attach event listeners Attribute binding: Vue's v-bind / Angular's [attr] - dynamically set attributes CSS binding: Vue's v-bind:class / Angular's [ngClass] - conditional classes
People like them because they move repetitive DOM manipulation patterns into declarative syntax. Instead of imperatively toggling display:none, you write v-show="isVisible". Instead of manually creating list elements, you write v-for="item in items".
For Chemistry, you could implement directives as methods on $Chemical that return modified JSX:
typescript
class $Chemical {
    $if(condition: boolean, element: ReactNode): ReactNode {
        return condition ? element : null;
    }
    
    $for<T>(items: T[], render: (item: T, index: number) => ReactNode): ReactNode {
        return items.map(render);
    }
    
    $show(condition: boolean, element: ReactElement): ReactElement {
        return React.cloneElement(element, {
            style: { ...element.props.style, display: condition ? '' : 'none' }
        });
    }
}
Then in views:
typescript
view() {
    return (
        <div>
            {this.$if(this.loaded, <Content />)}
            {this.$for(this.items, item => <Item data={item} />)}
        </div>
    );
}
Though Chemistry's reactive properties already handle most of what directives solve. The real value of directives is in template-based frameworks where you can't easily mix logic with markup. Since Chemistry uses JSX with full JavaScript, you already have {condition && <Element />} and {items.map(...)}.

Claude
15:48 UTC, 27 October 2025
Vue Directives
Rendering & Display:
v-if - Conditionally renders element (removes from DOM)
v-else-if - Chain conditional rendering
v-else - Fallback rendering
v-show - Toggles display CSS (keeps in DOM)
v-for - Renders lists/iterations
v-html - Sets innerHTML (dangerous)
v-text - Sets textContent
v-pre - Skip compilation for raw content
v-once - Render only once, skip updates
v-cloak - Hide until compiled
Data Binding:
v-model - Two-way binding for forms
v-bind (or :) - Bind attributes/props dynamically
Events:
v-on (or @) - Attach event listeners
Slots:
v-slot (or #) - Named/scoped slots
Angular Directives
Structural (modify DOM structure):
*ngIf - Conditional rendering
*ngFor - List rendering
*ngSwitch, *ngSwitchCase, *ngSwitchDefault - Switch statements
*ngTemplateOutlet - Render templates dynamically
*ngComponentOutlet - Render components dynamically
Attribute (modify appearance/behavior):
[ngClass] - Conditional CSS classes
[ngStyle] - Inline styles
[(ngModel)] - Two-way data binding
[hidden] - Hide elements
[disabled] - Disable elements
Event binding with (click), (change), etc.
Property binding with [property]
What React Does Instead
React doesn't have directives - it uses JavaScript expressions directly in JSX:
Conditional rendering: JavaScript logical operators (&&, ternary ? :)
Lists: JavaScript map() function
Two-way binding: Controlled components with value + onChange
Event handling: Direct event props (onClick, onChange)
CSS classes: Conditional strings or libraries like classnames
Styles: Style objects or conditional strings
Show/hide: Conditional rendering or style manipulation
Attributes: Direct prop spreading or conditional props
Templates/Slots: Component composition with props.children or render props
React's philosophy is "it's just JavaScript" - instead of learning directive syntax, you use JavaScript's built-in control flow and expressions. This makes React more verbose but also more explicit and flexible, since you have the full power of JavaScript rather than a predetermined set of directives.
The tradeoff: Vue/Angular are more concise for common patterns but require learning directive APIs. React requires more typing but uses concepts developers already know from JavaScript.

What how do event handlers work in react? onClick is a special prop?
Claude
15:50 UTC, 27 October 2025
Yes, onClick and other event handlers are special props in React, but not in the way you might think.
React implements its own event system called SyntheticEvents. When you write onClick, you're not directly setting a DOM onclick attribute. React:
Delegates all events - Instead of attaching listeners to individual DOM nodes, React attaches a single listener at the document root (or root container in React 17+)
Normalizes browser differences - SyntheticEvents wrap native browser events to provide consistent behavior across browsers
Pools events (pre-React 17) - Events were recycled for performance, which is why you couldn't use them asynchronously without calling persist()
Maps prop names to events - React knows that props matching the pattern on[EventName] are event handlers. It maps onClick to the click event, onChange to input/change events, etc.
Handles the event lifecycle - When an event fires on a DOM element, it bubbles up to React's root listener, which then:
Determines which component(s) should handle it
Creates/wraps the synthetic event
Calls your handler with the synthetic event
Handles propagation and default prevention
The special props React recognizes include onClick, onChange, onSubmit, onFocus, onBlur, onMouseEnter, onMouseLeave, onKeyDown, onKeyUp, and dozens more - basically camelCased versions of standard DOM events prefixed with "on".
React also handles some events specially - like onChange for inputs fires on every keystroke (unlike native DOM change which fires on blur), making controlled components easier to work with.
This is why you can't pass a string to onClick like in HTML (onclick="doThing()") - React expects an actual function reference because it's not setting an attribute, it's registering a handler in its event system.
Doug
15:50 UTC, 27 October 2025
But do all components support them? Or just the DOM api
Claude
15:51 UTC, 27 October 2025
Only DOM elements support event handler props directly. Custom React components don't automatically handle onClick or other event props unless they explicitly pass them through to DOM elements.
When you put onClick on a <button>, React knows to attach an event listener because button is a DOM element. But if you do <MyComponent onClick={handler} />, that onClick is just a regular prop to MyComponent. It won't trigger unless MyComponent internally does something like <div onClick={props.onClick}>.
This is actually a common source of confusion. People write <CustomButton onClick={doThing} /> and wonder why nothing happens. The CustomButton component needs to explicitly pass that onClick to an actual DOM element inside it.
React only treats props as event handlers when they're on lowercase (DOM) elements like div, button, input. On uppercase (component) elements, they're just props with no special meaning.
This is different from Vue/Angular where directives can work on any component. In React, only host elements (DOM nodes) have special prop behaviors. Everything else is just props that components can choose to use or ignore.
This separation is intentional - components have full control over their API. A component might choose to name its click handler onPress or handleClick instead of onClick. Or it might not support clicking at all. The component author decides, not the framework.

The parent swapping issue is a real problem. If a child chemical already has a parent and gets passed to another chemical's constructor, you have conflicting ownership. The child can't have two parents in the current model.
Your prototypal inheritance solution is architecturally elegant - it mirrors JavaScript's own object model at the component level. A chemical could have a prototype chain where:
The base chemical has the original bonds and properties
Each "instance" only stores its overrides
Property access walks up the chain until it finds a value
Setting a property creates a local override
This would let you share children across multiple parents without conflicts. Each parent would get what appears to be its own child, but they'd share underlying state except for explicitly overridden properties. Changes to shared properties propagate to all instances, but local overrides stay local.
The complexity comes in managing the bond system with this model. When a property changes on the prototype, all instances need to re-render. But when a local override changes, only that instance renders. The proxy system would need to track which properties are local versus inherited.
You'd also need to handle the parent reference specially. Maybe each prototypal instance has its own parent property that shadows the prototype's parent. This way a child can effectively have multiple "parent contexts" without conflict.
The revolutionary aspect is that this would enable true component reuse with variation - like CSS inheritance but for components. A list of items could share base behavior but have local customizations. Changing the prototype updates all instances unless they've overridden that specific property.
This pattern doesn't exist in other frameworks because they don't have Chemistry's object-oriented foundation. React's functional model and Vue's options API don't naturally support prototypal inheritance at the component instance level.
