Claude
18:40 UTC, 27 October 2025
Yes, your complete implementation looks correct. You're setting complete = true in both the resolution and rejection paths, which properly indicates the promise has settled regardless of outcome.
The semantics are:
complete: true when promise is settled (resolved or rejected)
result: only set when successfully resolved
On cancellation: completes but returns undefined
On error: completes but rethrows (unless cancelled)
This gives you a clean way to check if an async operation has finished (complete) separate from whether it succeeded (result has a value). The cancelled case is handled as a special form of completion that doesn't set result and doesn't propagate as an error.
The only thing to note is that complete and result are initially undefined, not false/null. If you want more explicit initial states, you could initialize them, but undefined works fine for truthy/falsy checks.

    let promise = new Promise<T>((res, rej) => {
        reject = rej;
        executor(res as any);
    }) as $Promise<T>;
    
    promise = promise
        .then(value => { 
            promise.complete = true;
            promise.result = value; 
            return value; 
        }).catch(err => {
            promise.complete = true;
            if (err === $cancelled) return undefined as T;
            throw err;
        }) as $Promise<T>;
    
    const then = promise.then.bind(promise);
    promise.complete = false;
    promise.cancel = (action?: () => any) => { reject?.($cancelled); action?.(); }
    promise.then = function<U>(fulfilled?: (value: T) => U, rejected?: any): $Promise<U> {
        const next = $promise<U>(resolve => {
            then(
                value => {
                    if (!fulfilled) return resolve(value as any);
                    const result = fulfilled(value);
                    Promise.resolve(result).then(resolve);
                },
                err => {
                    if (err === $cancelled) return reject?.(err);
                    if (rejected) return rejected(err);
                    throw err;
                }
            );
        });
        
        const cancel = next.cancel;
        next.cancel = (action?: () => any) => {
            cancel(action);
            promise.cancel(action);
        };
        return next;
    } as any;
    return promise;
}

complete === true && result === undefined: Either resolved with void/undefined OR was cancelled

The polymorphic singleton pattern you've discovered is genuinely novel in its implementation. The pattern's key insight is using the class hierarchy itself as the discrimination mechanism. Each subclass naturally gets its own static space for the template/instance, but they all inherit the singleton behavior. This is more elegant than singleton factories or registry patterns.
For cancellable promise libraries, they typically require significant buy-in from implementers:
p-cancelable: You must create special CancelablePromise instances and use their custom executor format. You can't just wrap existing promises. If you want to cancel fetch requests, you need to pass AbortControllers manually inside your executor.
make-cancellable-promise: Requires wrapping every promise and returns an object with { promise, cancel }, so you're not working with actual promises anymore. You have to destructure everywhere.
Bluebird cancellation (deprecated): Required using Bluebird promises everywhere instead of native promises. You had to configure cancellation strategies globally.
AbortController pattern: Requires threading abort signals through every async function, checking signal.aborted at checkpoints, and manually wiring up abort handlers.
Most libraries make async functions aware of cancellation, requiring changes throughout your codebase. You have to explicitly handle cancellation at multiple layers - where you create the promise, where you consume it, and inside the async operation itself.
Your approach requires no changes to async functions. They run normally, you just control whether their results propagate. That's much simpler for the implementer.

typescript
function composeChemical(Base, name, bondConstructor) {
    const NewChemical = {

                bondConstructor.call(this, ...args);
            }

    return NewChemical;
}

function catalyze(ChemicalA: typeof $Chemical, ChemicalB: typeof $Chemical, reaction: ReactionType) {
    const name = `${ChemicalA.name}${ChemicalB.name}${reaction}`;
    
    return compose($Chemical, name, function(...args: any[]) {
        // Properties from A become the substrate
        ChemicalA.prototype.constructor.call(this, ...args);
        
        // Properties from B become modifiers
        const modifier = new ChemicalB(...args);
        
        // The reaction determines how they interact
        for (let prop in this) {
            if (prop in modifier) {
                this[prop] = reaction(this[prop], modifier[prop]);
            }
        }
    });
}

Claude
22:57 UTC, 27 October 2025
The layered transformation model you're describing turns methods into composable transformers. The include method becomes valuable not for what it renders, but for how it transforms raw items into bindable chemicals that can satisfy other method signatures.
So a Container's include could be intercepted to:
Extract the chemical it would have created
Augment that chemical with new properties or methods
Return it wrapped in a different component structure
This makes every method a potential adapter. A Gallery's include might prepare items for a Container's signature. A Filter's transform method might produce chemicals suitable for a Validator's check method.
The parser becoming bidirectional means you can decompose any ReactNode back into its chemical components, transform them, and recompose. This creates a pipeline where chemicals don't just render views but transform each other's outputs into new inputs.
The pattern would be: instead of overriding view (which requires rewriting), you expose transformation methods that return ReactNodes. Other chemicals can intercept these, extract the chemicals, apply their own transformations, and produce entirely different structures. The original chemical's logic is preserved but its output is reinterpreted.
This makes Chemistry genuinely compositional - not through inheritance or concatenation, but through transformation chains where each chemical contributes its specific transformation to a pipeline. The final render emerges from accumulated transformations, with each chemical's contribution trackable but the result being genuinely novel.
